import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Conjecture 10.75

by V. P. Shunkov

Suppose that a group $G$ contains an element $a$ of prime order $p$ such that the
normalizer of every finite subgroup containing $a$ has finite periodic part and all
subgroups $\langle a, a^g \rangle$, $g \in G$, are finite and almost all of them are
soluble. Does $G$ possess a periodic part if $p > 2$?

It was proved in (V. P. Shunkov, *Groups with involutions*, Preprints no. 4, 5, 12 of the
Comput. centre of SO AN SSSR, Krasnoyarsk, 1986 (Russian)) that if $a$ is a point, then
the answer is affirmative; on the other hand, a group with a point $a$ of order 2
satisfying the given hypothesis, which has no periodic part, was exhibited in the same
works. For the definition of a *point* see (V. I. Senashov, V. P. Shunkov, *Algebra and
Logic*, **22**, no. 1 (1983), 66–81).

Here the *periodic part* of a group is the set of its elements of finite order, provided
this set is a subgroup; a group *possesses a periodic part* if this is the case. The
subgroup $\langle a, a^g \rangle$ is generated by $a$ and its conjugate $a^g = g^{-1} a g$.

*Reference:* [The Kourovka Notebook](https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v46)
-/

namespace Kourovka.«10.75»

/-- A group $G$ *possesses a periodic part* if the set of its elements of finite order
forms a subgroup of $G$ (this subgroup is then called the periodic part of $G$). -/
def HasPeriodicPart (G : Type*) [Group G] : Prop :=
  ∃ T : Subgroup G, ∀ x : G, x ∈ T ↔ IsOfFinOrder x

/-- A group possesses a periodic part if and only if the product of any two of its
elements of finite order has finite order. -/
@[category API, AMS 20]
theorem hasPeriodicPart_iff {G : Type*} [Group G] :
    HasPeriodicPart G ↔
      ∀ x y : G, IsOfFinOrder x → IsOfFinOrder y → IsOfFinOrder (x * y) := by
  constructor
  · rintro ⟨T, hT⟩ x y hx hy
    exact (hT _).1 (T.mul_mem ((hT x).2 hx) ((hT y).2 hy))
  · intro h
    exact ⟨{ carrier := {x | IsOfFinOrder x}
             one_mem' := IsOfFinOrder.one
             mul_mem' := fun hx hy => h _ _ hx hy
             inv_mem' := fun hx => hx.inv }, fun _ => Iff.rfl⟩

/-- Every abelian group possesses a periodic part, namely its torsion subgroup. -/
@[category test, AMS 20]
theorem hasPeriodicPart_of_commGroup (G : Type*) [CommGroup G] : HasPeriodicPart G :=
  ⟨CommGroup.torsion G, fun _ => Iff.rfl⟩

/-- Every periodic group possesses a periodic part, namely itself. -/
@[category test, AMS 20]
theorem hasPeriodicPart_of_isTorsion (G : Type*) [Group G] (h : Monoid.IsTorsion G) :
    HasPeriodicPart G :=
  ⟨⊤, fun x => ⟨fun _ => h x, fun _ => Subgroup.mem_top x⟩⟩

/-- The infinite dihedral group does not possess a periodic part: the product of the two
involutions $s$ and $sr$ is the element $r$ of infinite order. -/
@[category test, AMS 20]
theorem not_hasPeriodicPart_dihedralGroup_zero : ¬ HasPeriodicPart (DihedralGroup 0) := by
  rw [hasPeriodicPart_iff]
  intro h
  have h1 : IsOfFinOrder (DihedralGroup.sr 0 * DihedralGroup.sr 1 : DihedralGroup 0) :=
    h _ _ (orderOf_pos_iff.1 (by rw [DihedralGroup.orderOf_sr]; norm_num))
      (orderOf_pos_iff.1 (by rw [DihedralGroup.orderOf_sr]; norm_num))
  rw [DihedralGroup.sr_mul_sr, sub_zero] at h1
  exact orderOf_eq_zero_iff.1 DihedralGroup.orderOf_r_one h1

/--
Suppose that a group $G$ contains an element $a$ of prime order $p$ such that the
normalizer of every finite subgroup containing $a$ has finite periodic part and all
subgroups $\langle a, a^g \rangle$, $g \in G$, are finite and almost all of them are
soluble. Does $G$ possess a periodic part if $p > 2$?

"Almost all of the subgroups $\langle a, a^g \rangle$ are soluble" is formalized as: only
finitely many of the subgroups $\langle a, a^g \rangle$, $g \in G$, are not soluble.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 20]
theorem kourovka.«10.75» : answer(sorry) ↔
    ∀ (G : Type) [Group G] (p : ℕ) (a : G), p.Prime → 2 < p → orderOf a = p →
      (∀ H : Subgroup G, Finite H → a ∈ H →
        HasPeriodicPart H.normalizer ∧ {x : H.normalizer | IsOfFinOrder x}.Finite) →
      (∀ g : G, Finite (Subgroup.closure {a, g⁻¹ * a * g})) →
      {H : Subgroup G |
        ¬ IsSolvable H ∧ ∃ g : G, H = Subgroup.closure {a, g⁻¹ * a * g}}.Finite →
      HasPeriodicPart G := by
  sorry

end Kourovka.«10.75»

import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Conjecture 10.75

by V. P. Shunkov

Suppose that a group $G$ contains an element $a$ of odd prime order such that
the normalizer of every finite subgroup containing $a$ has only finitely many
elements of finite order. Suppose also that every subgroup
$\langle a, a^g\rangle$ is finite and all but finitely many distinct such
subgroups are soluble. Does the set of elements of finite order in $G$ form a
subgroup?

*Reference:* [The Kourovka Notebook](https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v46)
-/

namespace Kourovka.«10.75»

/--
Suppose that $a$ has prime order $p > 2$ in a group $G$. Assume that for every
finite subgroup $H$ containing $a$, only finitely many elements of the
normalizer $N_G(H)$ have finite order. Assume also that every
$\langle a, a^g\rangle$ is finite and that only finitely many distinct
subgroups $\langle a, a^g\rangle$ are non-soluble. Does the set of elements of
finite order in $G$ form a subgroup?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 20]
theorem kourovka.«10.75» : answer(sorry) ↔
    ∀ (G : Type) [Group G] (a : G) (p : ℕ),
      p.Prime → 2 < p → orderOf a = p →
      (∀ H : Subgroup G, (H : Set G).Finite → a ∈ H →
        Set.Finite {x : G | x ∈ H.normalizer ∧ IsOfFinOrder x}) →
      (∀ g : G,
        ((Subgroup.closure {a, g⁻¹ * a * g} : Subgroup G) : Set G).Finite) →
      Set.Finite {H : Subgroup G |
        (∃ g : G, H = Subgroup.closure {a, g⁻¹ * a * g}) ∧ ¬ IsSolvable H} →
      ∃ T : Subgroup G, (T : Set G) = {x : G | IsOfFinOrder x} := by
  sorry

end Kourovka.«10.75»
modeling_decisions: The group-theoretic conjugate a^g is represented explicitly as g⁻¹ * a * g.
“The normalizer has finite periodic part” is represented, as specified in the decomposition, by finiteness of the set of finite-order elements lying in the normalizer.

“Almost all” generated subgroups are soluble is represented by finiteness of the set of distinct subgroup values ⟨a, a^g⟩ that are not IsSolvable, rather than finiteness of the set of conjugating elements g producing a non-soluble subgroup.
“G possesses a periodic part” is represented by the existence of a subgroup whose carrier is exactly the set of finite-order elements of G.

namespace Kourovka.«10.75»

/-- A group $G$ *possesses a periodic part* if its elements of finite order form a subgroup.
This subgroup is then called the *periodic part* of $G$. -/
def HasPeriodicPart (G : Type*) [Group G] : Prop :=
  ∃ T : Subgroup G, ∀ x : G, x ∈ T ↔ IsOfFinOrder x

/-- A group $G$ *has finite periodic part* if its elements of finite order form a finite
subgroup. -/
def HasFinitePeriodicPart (G : Type*) [Group G] : Prop :=
  HasPeriodicPart G ∧ {x : G | IsOfFinOrder x}.Finite

/-- Every periodic (torsion) group possesses a periodic part, namely itself. -/
@[category API, AMS 20]
theorem HasPeriodicPart.of_isTorsion {G : Type*} [Group G] (h : Monoid.IsTorsion G) :
    HasPeriodicPart G :=
  ⟨⊤, fun x ↦ ⟨fun _ ↦ h x, fun _ ↦ Subgroup.mem_top x⟩⟩

/-- Every abelian group possesses a periodic part, namely its torsion subgroup. -/
@[category API, AMS 20]
theorem HasPeriodicPart.of_commGroup (G : Type*) [CommGroup G] : HasPeriodicPart G :=
  ⟨CommGroup.torsion G, CommGroup.mem_torsion G⟩

/-- Every finite group has finite periodic part. -/
@[category API, AMS 20]
theorem HasFinitePeriodicPart.of_finite (G : Type*) [Group G] [Finite G] :
    HasFinitePeriodicPart G :=
  ⟨HasPeriodicPart.of_isTorsion isOfFinOrder_of_finite, Set.toFinite _⟩

/-- The infinite dihedral group has no periodic part: it is generated by two involutions
whose product has infinite order. -/
@[category test, AMS 20]
theorem not_hasPeriodicPart_dihedralGroup_zero : ¬ HasPeriodicPart (DihedralGroup 0) := by
  rintro ⟨T, hT⟩
  have h0 : DihedralGroup.sr 0 ∈ T := (hT _).2 (isOfFinOrder_iff_pow_eq_one.2 ⟨2, by simp, by
    rw [pow_two, DihedralGroup.sr_mul_sr, sub_self, DihedralGroup.one_def]⟩)
  have h1 : DihedralGroup.sr 1 ∈ T := (hT _).2 (isOfFinOrder_iff_pow_eq_one.2 ⟨2, by simp, by
    rw [pow_two, DihedralGroup.sr_mul_sr, sub_self, DihedralGroup.one_def]⟩)
  have hr : DihedralGroup.r 1 ∈ T := by
    have := T.mul_mem h0 h1
    rwa [DihedralGroup.sr_mul_sr, sub_zero] at this
  have := orderOf_pos_iff.2 ((hT _).1 hr)
  rw [DihedralGroup.orderOf_r_one] at this
  exact lt_irrefl 0 this

Suppose that a group $G$ contains an element $a$ of prime order $p$ such that the
normalizer of every finite subgroup containing $a$ has finite periodic part and all
subgroups $\langle a, a^g \rangle$, $g \in G$, are finite and almost all of them are

means that the elements of finite order of $G$ form a subgroup.
-/

theorem kourovka.«10.75» : answer(sorry) ↔
    ∀ (G : Type) [Group G] (p : ℕ) (a : G), p.Prime → 2 < p → orderOf a = p →

      (∀ g : G, Finite (Subgroup.closure {a, g⁻¹ * a * g})) →
      {H : Subgroup G |
        (∃ g : G, H = Subgroup.closure {a, g⁻¹ * a * g}) ∧ ¬ IsSolvable H}.Finite →
      HasPeriodicPart G := by
  sorry

end Kourovka.«10.75»

/-- A group $G$ *possesses a periodic part* if the set of its elements of finite order
is a subgroup of $G$ (this subgroup is then called the periodic part of $G$). -/
def HasPeriodicPart (G : Type*) [Group G] : Prop :=
  ∃ T : Subgroup G, ∀ x, x ∈ T ↔ IsOfFinOrder x

/-- A group $G$ *has finite periodic part* if the set of its elements of finite order
is a finite subgroup of $G$. -/
def HasFinitePeriodicPart (G : Type*) [Group G] : Prop :=
  ∃ T : Subgroup G, (∀ x, x ∈ T ↔ IsOfFinOrder x) ∧ Finite T

theorem HasFinitePeriodicPart.hasPeriodicPart (h : HasFinitePeriodicPart G) :

  ⟨CommGroup.torsion A, fun _ => Iff.rfl⟩

attempts.decomposition_objections: None. The table already flags that the two 'point' variants depend on an external definition; I could not obtain it, so they are omitted rather than approximated.
modeling_decisions: 'G possesses a periodic part' is modeled as HasPeriodicPart G := ∃ H : Subgroup G, (H : Set G) = {g | IsOfFinOrder g}, i.e. the elements of finite order form a subgroup; G is not assumed infinite or periodic.

'the normalizer of every finite subgroup containing a has finite periodic part' is stated literally as: for every H : Subgroup G with Finite H and a ∈ H, HasPeriodicPart H.normalizer ∧ {x : H.normalizer | IsOfFinOrder x}.Finite. (By Dietzmann's lemma the first conjunct follows from the second, so this is equivalent to N_G(H) having only finitely many elements of finite order.)
a^g is taken as g⁻¹ * a * g (right conjugation, the notebook's convention); since g ranges over all of G the choice does not affect the statement.

'almost all of the subgroups ⟨a, a^g⟩ are soluble' is read, following the decomposition table, as: the set of subgroups {H | (∃ g, H = closure {a, g⁻¹ * a * g}) ∧ ¬ IsSolvable H} is finite (finitely many distinct non-soluble subgroups, not finitely many elements g).
Groups are quantified over Type (not Type*), following the existing Kourovka files.
Two short proved @[category API] lemmas (torsion groups and commutative groups have a periodic part) are included as basic tests of the bespoke definition, per CONTRIBUTING.md.
